sections.title: Against the grain
paragraphs: When you grow up curious and different in a place known for its repetitiveness and mediocrity, you eventually figure out that you want to run toward the exact things people say you can't do. For me, that was writing and marketing. People told me directly and indirectly that it wasn't a realistic path, which naturally meant I wanted to give it my all.

sections.title: Pulling at threads
paragraphs: I studied Computer Applications and started out as a content writer, with very little knowledge of the wider marketing discipline. I didn't stay in a single lane for long, not because I couldn't handle the writing, but because you can only write so many blogs before you start wondering where the landing page leads, how the campaign brings people there, and what the sales team is actually doing with the leads. I started pulling at those threads, which led me into SEO, website management, building sales decks, and go-to-market strategy. I call myself a marketing generalist now. It wasn't a grand career plan so much as a need to understand how the different pieces fit together, and I usually learn that by getting involved and doing the work myself.

sections.title: The bigger picture
paragraphs: I see marketing as orchestrating a play. There is a script, a set, lighting, actors, and a whole lot of work happening backstage. You can do a wonderful job with your specific part, but the production only works if all those elements talk to each other. I like being the person who can step into different roles when needed, rather than just watching from the audience. Working in lean, technology-focused teams has given me the room to operate like this. It showed me the actual value of taking ownership—having the freedom to step outside your job description and take responsibility for a project simply because a problem needs solving. Design is one of those areas I keep coming back to; I love it, and I will always find an excuse to figure out how an idea should look on a screen.

sections.title: Elsewhere
paragraphs: Lately, I am going back to where I started with coding. There is something satisfying about returning to a subject years later with a completely different set of problems in mind. I want to see how far I can take AI and code to automate the repetitive parts of marketing, experimenting with what I can build myself instead of always relying on off-the-shelf software. I am also helping a friend with their e-commerce business and exploring paid ads, adding to a list of things to learn that grows a lot faster than my ability to get around to them.

Outside of work, I spend my time reading classic philosophy and Kurt Vonnegut novels, or drinking cold brew while trying to get a double crochet stitch right. I am very much a beginner, so we'll see how that goes. I listen to Qawwali music, rewatch Schitt's Creek with absolutely no intention of stopping, and I've recently been exploring Rakhshan Banietemad's films alongside Rajnikanth's retro filmography (yes, the Jailer effect is real). None of this is meant to optimize my productivity or teach me a lesson about B2B SaaS, which is exactly why I do it.
